To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
, for the NJL model, the CEP is a second order critical point, and that, for the physical observables studied, the critical exponents are those of the three-dimensional Ising universality class.

(i) the order of the transition at the critical end point (the CEP) is first order, and (ii) the CEP is located in the region of small baryon chemical potential and low temperatures, at a value of the chemical potential that depends on the number of flavors.

, using the SU(3)-flavor NJL model, (i) the pressure and entropy show a smooth behavior around the CEP and (ii) the specific heat and baryon number susceptibilities show divergences that can be described by mean field exponents.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a better understanding of the QCD phase diagram and of its physical implications.
the study of the phase structure of strongly interacting matter at finite T and baryon number density, in the framework of the SU(3)xSU(3) NJL model.
the search for the QCD critical point in the (T, μB) plane.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the QCD phase transition at finite baryon density, in the vicinity of its CEP, has the following characteristics: the transition is of second order, and the chiral symmetry breaking is of mean field type, but the order parameter is not linear in the quark condensate.

, in the vicinity of CEP, the chiral symmetry is restored, and the transition is a second order transition with mean-field critical exponents, and the transition line between the hadronic and the quark‐gluon phase has the same critical exponents.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, although the order of the transition at the CEP is still an open question, the NJL model provides a consistent description of the chiral phase transitions at finite T and chemical potential, with a second order transition at zero chemical potential, and a crossover at finite chemical potential.
, although the NJL model is not able to describe correctly the phase transition at vanishing baryon density, it provides a reasonable description of the phase transition at finite density.
the CEP is not a second order transition point, but a weak first order transition point.
